topic: Design patterns for the three highest-traffic academic page types — Publications, People (current + alumni), Teaching — plus CV, News, Awards, Talks, Data/Code/Tools and Contact/Prospective-students, researched by fetching ~30 real faculty, lab and department sites (hydrology, civil engineering, CS/HCI, social science) and comparing them against Dr. Satish Regonda's existing Google Sites content.
key_findings: PUBLICATIONS — the single best detail found, and it comes from hydrology: Reed Maxwell's group site (https://maxwell.princeton.edu/) prints a one-line legend above 199 papers reading verbatim "(# indicates postdoc author, * indicates student author, ** indicates undergraduate student author, R.M.Maxwell in bold)". Real entries look like "Fleury*, M.P., Ma, Y., and **Maxwell, R.M.** High resolution estimates of water table depth across Brazil...". Three tiers of trainee marking + PI in bold, costs one line of CSS, and instantly communicates that the lab trains people.

PUBLICATIONS — title-first beats citation-first for scannability. Jesse Hahm's SFU hydrology group (https://jessehahm.github.io/) formats every entry as bold TITLE on line 1, authors + journal + year on line 2, then "(journal website)" and "(pdf)". Compare Satish's current page, which is pure citation-first APA — a wall of grey where the reader must parse past six author names to reach the topic.

PUBLICATIONS — link styling: the strongest sites use plain text separated by a slash or middot, NOT buttons. Jon Barron (https://jonbarron.info/) uses lowercase words joined by " / ": "project page / arXiv / video / code / bibtex". Kieran Healy (https://kieranhealy.org/publications/) uses a middot prefix: "· abstract  · pdf". Neither uses a pill, badge or coloured button. al-folio (https://alshedivat.github.io/al-folio/publications/) does use small buttons — "Abs", "Bib", "PDF", "HTML", "DOI" — and it reads busier.

PUBLICATIONS — venue is ITALIC, own name is BOLD. That split is near-universal in the good examples: Barron bolds "Jon Barron" and italicises "CVPR, 2025"; Healy italicises "Socio-Economic Review"; Maxwell bolds "Maxwell, R.M.". Nobody bolds the venue. Bolding both destroys the hierarchy.

PUBLICATIONS — the best answer to "100+ items without a wall of grey" is theme-counts as filter chips. MIT Visualization Group (https://vis.mit.edu/research/) heads its list with five theme chips carrying live counts — "Visualization Authoring Tools (27)", "Accessible Data Representations (17)", "Interpretability & Alignment (14)", "Cognitively Convivial Interaction (24)", "Sociocultural Design (8)" — plus a second row of method tags ("empirical study (13)", "qualitative methods (22)"), then year sections beneath. A ★ marks award papers.

PUBLICATIONS — Princeton CoCoSci (https://cocosci.princeton.edu/publications.php) handles hundreds of papers with year sections PLUS a colour-coded topic abbreviation tag stamped before each entry (e.g. [DMRL], [SML]) and a "View By Topic" switcher. The inline tag chip is what breaks the grey, more than the filter does.

PUBLICATIONS — Andrew Heiss (https://www.andrewheiss.com/research/) is the richest open-science link row found: per paper he offers "Full details »", "Preprint", "Final version", "Code", "Analysis notebook", "Data", "Replication Docker container", "Add to Zotero", plus 35 clickable topic tags in a sidebar and a haiku summary in place of an abstract. He splits by type: Journal articles / Working papers / Book chapters / Reviews / Dormant working papers.

PUBLICATIONS — citation metrics are a minority practice, not a norm. The peer-reviewed study "Citation personal display" (https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07960) sampled 870 physicists at 11 well-known universities and found only 14.8% (129/870) displayed citation counts on their personal sites; h-index display showed no significant variation by university, country or rank. Satish's Google Scholar (user=cTXdUlUAAAAJ) shows ~1,784 citations — a number that adds nothing and dates instantly.

PUBLICATIONS — the anti-pattern is widespread among senior hydrologists: Balaji Rajagopalan, Satish's own PhD advisor (https://civil.colorado.edu/~balajir/), publishes NO list at all, only the line "Publications can be obtained from - Google Scholar or Researcher ID". David Tarboton (https://hydrology.usu.edu/dtarb/) does the same via a bare link. Subimal Ghosh, IIT Bombay (https://www.civil.iitb.ac.in/~subimal/) is a contact card with a single "Detailed Information" link to a Wix site. Scilio's annotated review (https://www.scilio.app/examples) flags exactly this on Lauren DeLong's site: "There's no publication list on the site — visitors are routed to Google Scholar" with no curation or annotation.

PEOPLE / ALUMNI — the cleanest alumni line found, and it should be copied almost verbatim, is Bayani Cardenas's (https://www.jsg.utexas.edu/cardenas/people/): "Kevin Befus, PhD Geological Sciences, 2015 (Assistant Professor, University of Arkansas)" — name, degree, field, year, then current position in parentheses. No photo, one line, infinitely scalable. His section headings are explicitly "Former PhD Students, Post-doctoral Fellows, and Visiting Fellows", "Former MS/MA Students", "Former Undergraduate Students and REU/RET Fellows".

PEOPLE / ALUMNI — a TABLE beats cards once alumni exceed ~15. The Ying Hu Group at UIC (https://hu.lab.uic.edu/alumni/) uses four tables (Postdocs, PhD graduates, MS graduates, Undergraduates) with the PhD table carrying the column heading "Current position: Academia (A), Industry (I), Government (G)" alongside "Training period" and "Thesis". Sector-coding the placement is a credibility signal a plain list cannot give.

PEOPLE — "first placement" vs "current position" is a real fork. BU's Material Robotics Lab (https://sites.bu.edu/mrl/alumni) records only "first placement" for PhDs and postdocs (never goes stale, honest about what the lab caused). Pokhrel's MSU group (https://water.egr.msu.edu/members/) uses "**Current Position**: Postdoctoral scholar at KAUST, Saudi Arabia." (more impressive, but rots and requires chasing people).

PEOPLE — photos: current members get them, alumni almost never do. Cardenas, Hu Lab and BU MRL all show zero alumni photos; all show current-student headshots. This is the correct asymmetry — it also solves the fallback problem, because the group whose photos you can actually collect is the group standing in front of you. Where a photo is missing, the design-system answer is a deterministic initials monogram on a tinted square, never a blank box or a grey silhouette (setproduct.com/blog/avatar-ui-design: "Never leave the avatar blank").

TEACHING — the best structure found is Andrew Heiss's (https://www.andrewheiss.com/teaching/): reverse-chronological academic-year sections (2025–26 back to 2007–15); each course is ONE row carrying code + title ("PMAP 8551/4551"), institution, a one-sentence description ("Use R, ggplot2, and the principles of graphic design to create beautiful and truthful visualizations of data"), and then EVERY semester it was taught as a separate link — "Fall 2025", "Spring 2026". Repeat offerings become links on one row instead of duplicate rows.

TEACHING — Kieran Healy (https://kieranhealy.org/teaching/) uses a single scrolling page and tells you so: "the further you scroll down the page the further into the past you will travel." Current courses get a paragraph and a live course site; past courses collapse to title + syllabus PDF. That progressive decay of detail is the right model for a professor with a decade of repeats.

TEACHING — a teaching-philosophy statement works when it is specific and tool-named, not aspirational. The Kasprzyk Research Group at CU Boulder (https://www.colorado.edu/lab/krg/teaching/teaching-philosophy) lists CVEN 4333 Engineering Hydrology (~100 students, juniors/seniors), CVEN 5393 Water Resource Systems and Management (~15–20 grads), CVEN 5423, names the actual software (RiverWare, Python), names a case study (Colorado River negotiations), and then covers mentoring separately (conference travel, weekly interdisciplinary workshops, public-speaking feedback). Enrolment numbers and level are cheap and highly informative.

PROSPECTIVE STUDENTS — the highest-value page on the whole site, and the current one is under-specified. The best patterns state funding reality FIRST. The Remote Sensing Hydrology group's page (https://www.remote-sensing-hydrology.com/prospective-students, PI identity UNVERIFIED) front-loads "I do not currently have funding for a graduate student", routes everyone through a Google Form instead of email, and includes an optional question asking the applicant to pick one of his papers and answer questions on it. Mark Dean (https://markdean.info/openings/) writes "We do not currently have open postdoc positions, but interested candidates are welcome to email Mark. We especially welcome postdocs with fellowships, and would be happy to support you in applying both before and after joining our group", then lists named fellowship schemes by country.

PROSPECTIVE STUDENTS — UVA's Security Research Group (https://uvasrg.github.io/prospective/) is the canonical structured guide: sections "Who To Contact", "Do Your Homework", "First Email", "What Not To Do", "Follow Up". Core instruction: "read the advisor's home page...and at least one recent paper"; keep the email to "approximately one screenful"; explicitly do NOT send GPA/GRE scores, attachments, or fancy formatting. Yonatan Bisk's FAQ (https://talkingtorobots.com/FAQ.html) publishes the actual admissions funnel as a table (two 50% filtering rounds before faculty see ~25%) — demystifying the process is itself a kindness.

SITE ARCHITECTURE — the personal-site / group-site split has a proven shape that maps exactly onto satishregonda.in + raftwaters.in. Arvind Satyanarayan (https://arvindsatya.com/) keeps a deliberately thin personal page — photo, three paragraphs, links — and states "Please consult my research group's website for our latest publications and active projects." The opposite model is Mark Dean (https://markdean.info/), a personal site that scales INTO a group site with nav "About / People / Group notes / Research / Openings / Publications / Preprints" and a ctrl-K search. Given RAFT will be hosted separately, Satish's site must be self-sufficient (own publications, own students) and treat RAFT as a rich single page that hands off, not as the home of the content.

NEWS — the format that works is a dated one-liner list, 4–6 items visible, reverse chronological, each linking somewhere. Mark Dean's homepage runs four items dated to within days: "Mark is attending the MAIQmag All Hands Meeting at Oak Ridge National Laboratory on August 24–25." Scilio's review is blunt about the failure mode — Martin Bulla's site displays a "last updated" date and that date itself had gone stale — and concludes for Andrew Heiss's site that "an honest paragraph beats an outdated news feed."

CONTACT — Satish's own contact data is currently INCONSISTENT ACROSS SOURCES, which is a live bug the new site must fix. His Google Site says "Tel: +91-40-2301 6315" and "Kandi - 502285"; the IITH departmental profile (https://iith.ac.in/ce/satishr/) says "(040) 2359 - 6315", "Room: B-212, Department of Civil Engineering", "Kandi-502284, Sangareddy, Telangana, India". Two different phone numbers and two different PIN codes.

DATA/CODE — Satish already has the strongest possible content for this section and it is currently buried under the label "Products" at the top of his publications page: a climate analysis web tool, Hydro-EMOS (streamflow forecasting diagnostic tool) and a poverty visualization app. Reed Maxwell gives ParFlow and EcoSLIM their own top-level "codes" nav item with GitHub links; that is the correct promotion.
recommendations: Build the publications page title-first, not citation-first. Line 1: paper title in a slightly larger serif/medium weight (linked to DOI). Line 2: author list at ~0.9rem in a muted grey, with "Regonda, S.K." in the body-text colour at medium weight so it pops without shouting. Line 3: journal in italic + volume + year. Line 4: a thin row of lowercase text links separated by " · " — doi · pdf · data · code · press. Follow Hahm (https://jessehahm.github.io/) for the shape and Barron (https://jonbarron.info/) for the separator discipline.

Adopt Maxwell's trainee-marking legend, adapted for an Indian institute, and print it once at the top of the publications page in small caps: "* PhD student · † M.Tech student · ‡ B.Tech student · # postdoc — supervised in my group. Regonda, S.K. set in bold." Use a superscript symbol immediately after the student's surname. This single detail does more for the professor's reputation as a mentor than any prose paragraph, and it is the kind of thing an AI-generated template never has.

Do NOT split "Selected" and "All" into two pages. Use one page with a filter chip row above the year sections, seeded from the paper's own theme tag: e.g. "All (39) · Urban flooding (11) · Streamflow forecasting (9) · Monsoon & climate variability (8) · Reservoir & water management (6) · Data & tools (5)". Counts come free from the sheet. Add a single ★ or a hairline left rule to ~6 papers he marks as "selected" in the sheet, and default the homepage to showing only those six. Pattern from https://vis.mit.edu/research/ and https://cocosci.princeton.edu/publications.php.

Ship a client-side text filter, not a search engine. With ~39 journal papers, ~4 book chapters and ~20+ conference items, one input box that hides non-matching rows on keyup (matching title + authors + journal + year) is 25 lines of vanilla JS and covers 100% of the real use case ("did he publish with X?", "what did he do on Godavari?"). The MIT DLC template (https://sites.mit.edu/dlc-template-6/publications) uses "Search publications:" + a type dropdown + a year dropdown + "Reset filters" — copy the labels, drop the dropdowns.

Offer BibTeX as an inline expand, not a modal and not a separate page. A "bib" text link that toggles a monospace <pre> block directly beneath the entry, with a small "copy" affordance in its corner. al-folio's "Bib" button opening an expandable BibTeX block (https://alshedivat.github.io/al-folio/publications/) is the reference implementation; Mark Dean (https://markdean.info/publications/) does the same. Generate the BibTeX at build time from the sheet columns so the professor never touches LaTeX.

Show no citation counts, no h-index, no journal impact factors anywhere on the site. Instead put one quiet link row under the bio: "Google Scholar · ORCID · ResearchGate · IRINS". Evidence: only 14.8% of physicists at 11 leading universities display citations on personal pages (https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07960), and any number hard-coded into a static site is wrong within a month.

For PEOPLE, use two different visual systems on one page: current members as a photo grid (soft-cornered square photos, ~140px, name / degree programme / cohort year / one-line topic / optional co-advisor / optional links), and alumni as compact one-line rows in the Cardenas format — "Name, PhD Civil Engineering, 2023 — Thesis title — (now: Scientist, NRSC Hyderabad)". See https://www.jsg.utexas.edu/cardenas/people/ and https://hu.lab.uic.edu/alumni/.

Make the alumni field "first position after graduating" in the sheet, and label it on the page as such where it is old (BU MRL model, https://sites.bu.edu/mrl/alumni). Add an optional second column "currently" that renders only when filled. This means the page is never wrong and never requires the professor to chase former students annually.

Add a one-line summary strip above the alumni list — "12 PhD and M.Tech theses completed since 2017. Alumni are at NRSC, CWC, IITs, and in industry." — because that sentence is the actual credibility payload and most visitors will not read 30 rows. UIC's academia/industry/government sector-coding (https://hu.lab.uic.edu/alumni/) is the more granular version of the same idea.

Handle missing student photos with a deterministic initials monogram: two letters, centred, on a tinted square derived from a hash of the name, using the site's own accent hue at low saturation so the grid never looks broken. Never a grey silhouette, never a blank slot, never a stock photo. Guidance: https://www.setproduct.com/blog/avatar-ui-design.

For TEACHING, restructure his flat bullet list of ten course names into rows of: COURSE CODE — Course name — level badge (B.Tech / M.Tech / PhD) — one-sentence description — then semester chips ("Aug 2024", "Jan 2023", "Aug 2021") as links or plain text. Group under "Currently teaching" and "Previously taught". Exact model: https://www.andrewheiss.com/teaching/. Course codes must be obtained from IITH — his current page has none, which makes the list unusable to a student looking up a course.

Write a short teaching statement of 120–180 words that names software and datasets (R, Shiny, Google Earth Engine, HEC-RAS/HEC-HMS, drone imagery, Indian gauge data) and gives approximate class sizes and levels, following https://www.colorado.edu/lab/krg/teaching/teaching-philosophy. Put mentoring, outreach and service in a separate short block below it, not mixed in.

Do NOT link to the institutional LMS. It is authenticated, it breaks for outsiders, and it is the single most common dead link on faculty teaching pages. Link instead to a static per-course page on this site holding syllabus PDF, topic outline, reading list, and any public slides/notebooks — and only for the two or three courses he actually wants to showcase.

Make the CV a PDF that is generated from the same Google Sheets the site reads, and stamp the page with the generation date: "Curriculum Vitae (PDF, updated 4 September 2026)". Also render a lightweight HTML CV page for SEO and for people on phones. The rule from every source: one source of record, many renderings — never a hand-maintained PDF plus a hand-maintained page, which drift within one semester.

Give Talks its own page, grouped by year, each row: talk title (or "Invited seminar"), host institution or conference, city, month-year, and an optional "slides" / "video" link. Keep keynotes and plenaries visually distinguished with a small label rather than a separate section — Nuria Oliver's three-way categorisation (https://nuriaoliver.com/invitedtalks.htm) fragments the timeline and makes it hard to see recency. His existing "Invited Seminars" and "Presentations at Conferences" sections already hold this data.

Promote his "Products" out of the publications page into a top-level section named "Tools" or "Data & Tools": one card each for the climate analysis web tool, Hydro-EMOS, the poverty visualization app, and SnapFlood, with a screenshot, two-sentence description of who it is for, a live link, and a GitHub link if any. This is his strongest differentiator versus every other hydrology faculty page and it is currently invisible. Model: the "codes" nav item at https://maxwell.princeton.edu/.

Rewrite the Contact page around the one question he is actually emailed about. Structure: (1) office room B-212, department, full postal address, phone, email — reconciled to a single verified set, since https://iith.ac.in/ce/satishr/ and his Google Site currently disagree on both phone number and PIN code; (2) a heading "Prospective students and postdocs" carrying current funding/vacancy status as a dated line, what backgrounds fit, and the exact email subject line to use; (3) a short "what to put in your email" list; (4) a line on what he cannot do (review CVs for unrelated programmes, write letters for people he has not taught). Models: https://markdean.info/openings/ and https://uvasrg.github.io/prospective/.

Keep his existing subject-line convention — the current Opportunities page already asks candidates to write "Looking for an Opportunity" — but strengthen it into a required, copy-to-clipboard string, and add the paper-engagement test from https://www.remote-sensing-hydrology.com/prospective-students: ask applicants to name one paper of his they read and one question it raised. It filters mass-mailers at zero cost.

Put a dated news list of 5 items on the homepage with a "more →" to an archive, and drive it from one sheet with columns date / text / optional link. Add an explicit "Last updated" stamp in the footer generated at build time, so it can never be stale in the way Scilio caught on martinbulla.github.io (https://www.scilio.app/examples).

Design the Google Sheets schema now, because it determines what the design can render. Publications: id | year | type | title | authors_raw | author_marks | journal | volume | pages | doi | pdf_url | code_url | data_url | press_url | theme | selected(Y/N) | note. People: name | role | programme | cohort_year | topic | co_advisor | photo_file | email | scholar | website | status(current/alumni) | end_year | thesis_title | first_position | current_position | order. Teaching: code | title | level | semesters (comma list) | description | syllabus_url | site_url | status. Keep one tab per type, freeze the header row, and validate on build so a typo shows as a build error rather than a broken page.
pitfalls: Delegating publications to Google Scholar. Balaji Rajagopalan's site (https://civil.colorado.edu/~balajir/) says only "Publications can be obtained from - Google Scholar or Researcher ID" and David Tarboton's (https://hydrology.usu.edu/dtarb/) does the same. Scilio's reviewers flag this explicitly as a failure — it surrenders all curation, all student credit, and all theme grouping, and it is exactly what a professor with an existing Scholar profile is tempted to do.

Button soup. Once every link becomes a filled pill — PDF, DOI, Code, Data, Slides, Video, BibTeX, Cite, Press — a 40-paper page becomes 200 coloured rectangles and the titles disappear. al-folio's Abs/Bib/PDF/HTML/DOI row already reads busy at demo scale. Use lowercase text links separated by a middot, at ~0.8rem in a muted colour, and let only the paper title carry visual weight.

Bolding the journal name. It competes with the title and the author's own name and produces three levels of bold in one entry. Every good exemplar italicises the venue and bolds only the site owner's name.

Showing citation counts or h-index. Statistically it is a minority behaviour (14.8% of 870 physicists, https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.07960); on a static site it is guaranteed to be stale; and on a mid-career Indian faculty page it reads defensive rather than confident.

Photo grids for alumni. As the group grows, missing headshots for people who left in 2018 will create permanent holes, and chasing 30 former students for photos is a job nobody will do. Every alumni exemplar found (Cardenas, UIC Hu Lab, BU MRL) uses text rows and none uses photos.
"Current position" for alumni without a review process. It is impressive on day one and wrong within two years. Prefer "first position after graduating", with "currently" as an optional extra field.

Linking the institutional LMS (Moodle/Google Classroom) from the teaching page. It is behind auth, it 404s between semesters, and it makes the page look abandoned to the external visitor the page exists for.
Duplicating a course row for every semester it was taught. Ten courses across nine years becomes forty rows of near-identical text. Heiss's one-row-many-semester-links pattern avoids it entirely.

A "Lab Pets" section or similar whimsy. Sinclair Lab (https://sinclairlab.rice.edu/people) lists two cats as "Purr Reviewer #1" and "Purr Reviewer #2". Charming for a US psychology lab, wrong register for an IIT civil engineering professor and a government-facing flood forecasting group.

A news feed the professor will not feed. Scilio's review catches sites where the "last updated" line is itself out of date, and concludes for one site that "an honest paragraph beats an outdated news feed." If updates land less than monthly, use a short "What I'm working on now" paragraph plus a build-time date stamp rather than a timeline that visibly stops.
Two CVs. A hand-edited PDF and a hand-edited HTML CV page will diverge — usually the PDF gets updated for a grant deadline and the page does not. Generate both, or ship only the PDF with a date.

Publishing contact details without reconciling them first. The site currently would inherit a phone/PIN-code contradiction between his Google Site and https://iith.ac.in/ce/satishr/ — publishing both is worse than publishing neither.

Making satishregonda.in depend on raftwaters.in for its substance. raftwaters.in does not currently resolve (DNS lookup failed, 4 Sep 2026 — UNVERIFIED whether it is registered but unhosted). The RAFT page must be a complete, self-contained account of the group with an outbound link, so the site never has a dead centre.

Treating listicles as design research. The founderjar roundup (https://www.founderjar.com/inspiration/academic-website-examples/) recommends parallax scrolling, image sliders, hero animations and hamburger-only navigation — every one of which is wrong for a research site whose visitors arrive to find a specific paper, student or course.

Abstract-expanders on every paper. They double the DOM, they are rarely opened, and they push the next title below the fold. Heiss replaces the abstract with a haiku; Barron shows none at all; Naik's page (https://www.anaikowl.com/publications) shows none despite being praised for "publications with abstracts". A one-line plain-English takeaway written by the professor, on the ~6 selected papers only, is worth far more than 39 collapsed abstracts.

exemplars.name: Reed Maxwell, Princeton University (Maxwell Integrated Hydrology Group)
exemplars.what_works: Single-page group site with nav "maxwell lab / about reed / research / education and outreach / group / publications / codes". 199 publications in one list, headed by an explicit legend. "codes" is a top-level nav item giving ParFlow and EcoSLIM equal billing with papers. Education and outreach is a first-class section naming STEM fairs, local schools and a Digital Sandtank tool, alongside "CEE 306 / ENV 318 Hydrology: Water and Climate (Spring)".
exemplars.steal_this: The co-author legend, verbatim in structure: "(# indicates postdoc author, * indicates student author, ** indicates undergraduate student author, R.M.Maxwell in bold)" — adapted to PhD / M.Tech / B.Tech / postdoc tiers for an Indian institute.

exemplars.name: W. Jesse Hahm, Simon Fraser University (SFU Hydrology Research Group)
exemplars.what_works: Anchor-linked single page: Research Statement, Teaching, People, Publications, Outreach, Contact. Serif headings over sans body, large images between sections. Teaching lists four courses with brief descriptions and links to official outlines. Outreach is a media-mentions list (Scientific American, Nature Geoscience, NYT) that quietly demonstrates impact.
exemplars.steal_this: The title-first publication entry: bold title on line one, "Shotayo, Allen, Hahm. Hydrological Processes, 2026." on line two, then "(journal website)" and "(pdf)". Also the Outreach-as-press-mentions section, which is far better use of space than a press-logo wall.

exemplars.name: Andrew Heiss, Georgia State University
exemplars.what_works: Publications grouped by type (Journal articles / Working papers / Book chapters / Reviews / Dormant working papers / Selected seminar papers / Translations) with a 35-tag topic sidebar. Every entry carries a contextual resource row: "Full details »", "Preprint", "Final version", "Code", "Analysis notebook", "Data", "Replication Docker container", "Add to Zotero". Site nav is About / CV / Blog / Research / Teaching / Talks / Now / Uses / AI.
exemplars.steal_this: The per-paper resource row that varies by paper rather than showing empty slots, and the honesty of a "Dormant working papers" category. Also the "»" affordance instead of a button.

exemplars.name: Andrew Heiss — teaching page
exemplars.what_works: Academic-year sections (2025–26 down to 2007–15). One row per course carrying code ("PMAP 8551/4551"), institution, a single-sentence description, and each semester it ran as a separate link to that semester's course website. Plus an "Interactive resources" section for teaching tools he built.
exemplars.steal_this: One course row, many semester links. It compresses a decade of repeat teaching into a scannable list and is exactly what Satish's ten-bullet course list needs.

exemplars.name: MIT Visualization Group (Arvind Satyanarayan)
exemplars.what_works: Publications organised by year but headed by two rows of filter chips carrying live counts — five research themes ("Visualization Authoring Tools (27)" … "Sociocultural Design (8)") and seven method tags ("empirical study (13)", "qualitative methods (22)"). Card layout with left thumbnail, ★ for award papers, icon links to PDF / project site / GitHub, occasional embedded video.
exemplars.steal_this: Theme chips with counts in parentheses. They turn a long list into a map of the research programme and make the professor's areas legible in two seconds.

exemplars.name: M. Bayani Cardenas, UT Austin (Cardenas Hydrology Research Group)
exemplars.what_works: Eight explicit sections including "MS Students (currently none)" — honest about a shrinking cohort rather than hiding the heading. Current students get a headshot, both degrees with institutions, 1–3 paragraphs of research interests, and personal interests. Alumni get one text line each.
exemplars.steal_this: The alumni line format exactly: "Kevin Befus, PhD Geological Sciences, 2015 (Assistant Professor, University of Arkansas)" — and the willingness to keep an empty category heading visible so the group's shape is always readable.

exemplars.name: Ying Hu Group, University of Illinois Chicago
exemplars.what_works: Four tables by degree level. The PhD table's columns are "Current position: Academia (A), Industry (I), Government (G)", "Training period", "Thesis" — thesis titles in full, no photos, chronological within level.
exemplars.steal_this: Sector-coding the placement (A/I/G). For an Indian hydrology group, an equivalent coding — academia / government agency (CWC, IMD, NRSC, state irrigation) / industry / consulting — would be an unusually strong credibility signal.

exemplars.name: Mark P. M. Dean, Brookhaven National Laboratory
exemplars.what_works: A personal site that scales into a group site: nav is About / People / Group notes / Research / Openings / Publications / Preprints, with ctrl-K search. News is 4 dated one-liners updated within days. Publications and Preprints are separate top-level sections; publications are numbered within each year and offer DOI / Bib (expandable BibTeX) / PDF / Supp, with the PI bolded in author lists.
exemplars.steal_this: "Openings" as a top-level nav item rather than buried text — it recruits continuously — and the expandable inline BibTeX block.

exemplars.name: Mark Dean — openings page
exemplars.what_works: Leads with the negative and stays welcoming: "We do not currently have open postdoc positions, but interested candidates are welcome to email Mark. We especially welcome postdocs with fellowships, and would be happy to support you in applying both before and after joining our group." Then lists named fellowship schemes by country.
exemplars.steal_this: State current funding reality first, then name the specific external fellowships (for India: PMRF, CSIR/UGC-JRF, DST INSPIRE, N-PDF, Fulbright-Nehru, Newton-Bhabha) an applicant could bring.

exemplars.name: UVA Security Research Group (David Evans) — advice for prospective students
exemplars.what_works: Seven sections: intro, "Who To Contact", "Do Your Homework", "First Email", "What Not To Do", "Follow Up", "Conclusion". Concrete rules: read the home page and at least one recent paper; keep the email to about one screenful; name the paper and where you found it; end with one clear question. Explicit don'ts: no GPA/GRE scores, no attachments, no generic flattery, no fancy formatting.
exemplars.steal_this: The "What Not To Do" section. Publishing it publicly saves the professor hundreds of emails a year and is genuinely generous to applicants.

exemplars.name: Joseph Kasprzyk Research Group, CU Boulder — teaching philosophy
exemplars.what_works: Names three courses with codes, approximate enrolment and level (CVEN 4333 Engineering Hydrology, ~100 students, juniors/seniors; CVEN 5393, ~15–20 grads; CVEN 5423). Names the actual tools (RiverWare, Python) and a real case study (Colorado River negotiations). Mentoring is separated out: public-speaking feedback, conference travel, weekly interdisciplinary workshops.
exemplars.steal_this: Enrolment size + student level per course, and splitting "mentoring" from "teaching" so graduate advising gets its own paragraph.

exemplars.name: Yaoping Wang / Yadu Pokhrel Multi-scale FEW Systems Modeling Lab, Michigan State
exemplars.what_works: Six member categories including "Visiting Researchers/Interns" and "Past Group Members" subdivided by role. Each alumnus ends with a bolded label — "**Current Position**: Postdoctoral scholar at KAUST, Saudi Arabia." or "**Currently at**: Jacobs Solutions Inc."
exemplars.steal_this: The dedicated "Visiting Researchers / Interns" category — highly relevant for an IIT group that hosts summer interns and project staff who would otherwise be invisible.

exemplars.name: Jon Barron, Google DeepMind
exemplars.what_works: One reverse-chronological list, 2008–2026, no selected/all split, no counts, no metrics. Own name bold, venue italic ("CVPR, 2025"), accent tags like "(Oral Presentation)" and "(Highlight)" in bold. Every paper has before/after thumbnails or a short video. Links are lowercase words joined by " / ": "project page / arXiv / video / code / bibtex".
exemplars.steal_this: The slash-separated lowercase link string. It carries six links with less visual noise than two buttons would.

exemplars.name: Kieran Healy, Duke University
exemplars.what_works: Grouped by type — Books, Working Papers, Retired Papers, Articles and Book Chapters, Essays and Reviews. Venue italic, title plain. Each entry gets exactly two links prefixed with a middot: "· abstract  · pdf". Prominent link to "Full Curriculum Vitae in pdf format" at the top. Teaching page is one scroll with the line "the further you scroll down the page the further into the past you will travel."
exemplars.steal_this: "Retired Papers" as a named category, and the middot-prefixed two-link discipline. Also: putting the CV PDF link at the top of the publications page, where people looking for the full record actually are.

exemplars.name: Princeton Computational Cognitive Science Lab
exemplars.what_works: Hundreds of papers, grouped by year, with a "View By Topic" switcher across ~13 topic areas and a colour-coded topic abbreviation stamped inline before each entry (e.g. [DMRL], [SML]). Author names are clickable to see that person's full output.
exemplars.steal_this: The inline colour-coded topic chip. It is what visually breaks up a long list — more effective than the filter itself — and it lets a reader scan for a theme without interacting.

exemplars.name: Sinclair Lab, Rice University
exemplars.what_works: Two orthogonal filter axes presented as linked categories: Research Topics ("Learning & Memory", "Motivation & Emotion", "Belief & Behavior Change", "Information Consumption") and Application Domains ("Education", "Health Behavior", "Climate Change", "Science Communication"). Per paper: title, authors with PI bolded, full venue with volume/issue/pages, "View PDF" and "Link".
exemplars.steal_this: Two filter axes — method/topic and application domain. For Satish this maps cleanly onto (streamflow forecasting, urban flooding, monsoon variability, statistical methods) × (Hyderabad, Godavari/Krishna basins, national scale, operational agencies).

exemplars.name: al-folio Jekyll theme demo
exemplars.what_works: Year headers, left thumbnail, small button row "Abs / Bib / DOI / HTML / PDF / Video", site owner's name italicised automatically, co-author names auto-linked from a coauthors data file, award badges. Generated entirely from a .bib file.
exemplars.steal_this: The idea, not the styling: derive author-name emphasis and co-author links automatically from structured data so the professor never hand-formats a citation. Its button row is the thing to avoid.

exemplars.name: Mayank Mittal (ETH Zurich / NVIDIA)
exemplars.what_works: Each publication is a mini-project: left-aligned animated GIF teaser, title, author list with collaborator links, venue+year ("RSS 2026"), a 2–4 sentence plain description, then monospace bracket links "[Abs] [arXiv] [Website] [Video] [Code]". Dated news timeline above the publications in MMM DD, YYYY format.
exemplars.steal_this: The 2–4 sentence plain-language description under each featured paper. For a flood-forecasting group whose audience includes agency engineers and journalists, this is more valuable than an abstract.

exemplars.name: Nicole Paul (ETH Zürich)
exemplars.what_works: Chronological list filterable by publication type (Journal article / Conference paper / Report) and date, with a consistent per-paper resource row: PDF, Cite, DOI, Dataset, Code, Project, Slides — rendered as plain text links in a horizontal row with no colour or fill.
exemplars.steal_this: Dataset and Slides as first-class per-paper links, and the restraint of rendering all of them as undifferentiated plain text.

exemplars.name: Arvind Satyanarayan (MIT)
exemplars.what_works: A deliberately thin personal page — one photo, three paragraphs, contact icons — that explicitly hands off: "Please consult my research group's website for our latest publications and active projects." Career materials archived by milestone (tenure 2024, mid-tenure 2021, job search 2016).
exemplars.steal_this: The clean handoff sentence — but as a cautionary model. Because raftwaters.in is separately hosted and does not currently resolve, satishregonda.in must NOT adopt this thinness; it needs its own complete publications and people pages, with RAFT as a rich page that links out.

exemplars.name: Scilio — 12 annotated academic websites (2026)
exemplars.what_works: Twelve real sites reviewed with named strengths, weaknesses and a takeaway each. Diagnoses that recur: routing visitors to Google Scholar instead of curating your own list; stale copyright years and dead news feeds; skills claimed without clickable evidence; publication types that blur together visually.
exemplars.steal_this: The maintenance-first framing: choose a structure the professor can actually keep current. It is the strongest argument for the Google Sheets pipeline and for a build-time "last updated" stamp.

exemplars.name: IIT Hyderabad Civil Engineering — Satish Regonda's institutional profile
exemplars.what_works: Canonical institutional record: Associate Professor, Civil Engineering and Climate Change, "Room: B-212, Department of Civil Engineering", "Indian Institute of Technology Hyderabad, Kandi-502284, Sangareddy, Telangana, India", "(040) 2359 - 6315", satishr@ce.iith.ac.in, research interests listed as Urban and Rural Flood Modeling, Climate Sciences, Data Sciences, Statistical Modeling Techniques, Ensemble Forecasting, Multiscale Modelling, AI/ML.
exemplars.steal_this: Use this as the authority for office, address and phone — and reconcile it against the Google Site, which currently gives a different phone (+91-40-2301 6315) and a different PIN (502285).

details:
## Method

I fetched ~30 live pages and ran ~14 searches. Every URL in `exemplars` returned real content. Sites that failed to fetch and are therefore NOT cited as exemplars: `timalthoff.com` (TLS), `amir.aghakouchak.com` (TLS), `hydrox.iitd.ac.in` and `hpmlab.iitd.ac.in` and `web.iitd.ac.in/~dhanya/` (untrusted certificate), `idl.uw.edu/papers` (404), `vis.csail.mit.edu/pubs` (Apache directory index only), `hydro.esci.umn.edu/people` (403), `madeline-eppley.com` (JS-only shell), `hydrogeology.msu.edu/people/lab-members` (empty), `sites.google.com/a/iitgn.ac.in/water-and-climate-change` (auth wall — Vimal Mishra's lab site is behind a Google login, worth noting as a failure mode of Google Sites).

**`raftwaters.in` does not resolve** — DNS `ENOTFOUND` as of 4 Sep 2026. UNVERIFIED whether it is registered-but-unhosted or not yet registered. Design implication below.

---

## 1. PUBLICATIONS

### 1.1 Grouping: what the field actually does

| Site | Grouping | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| jonbarron.info | Pure reverse-chron, 2026→2008, one list | No selected/all split, no counts |
| kieranhealy.org | By **type**: Books / Working Papers / Retired Papers / Articles and Book Chapters / Essays and Reviews | Type-first suits a book-writing discipline |
| andrewheiss.com | By type (7 categories) + 35-tag topic sidebar | Richest hybrid |
| vis.mit.edu | Year sections + theme chips with counts on top | Best for a programme with distinct threads |
| cocosci.princeton.edu | Year sections + inline colour topic tags + "View By Topic" | Best for very high volume |
| markdean.info | Year sections, **numbered within year**, Publications and Preprints as separate pages | |
| maxwell.princeton.edu | One flat list of 199 | Works because of the legend and the numbering; still greyish |
| sinclairlab.rice.edu | Two filter axes: Research Topics × Application Domains | |
| nicolepaul.io | Chron + type filter + date filter | |
| Satish's current page | Sections A–F: Products / In Referred Journals / Book Chapters / Presentations at Conferences / Invited Seminars / Scientific activities; reverse-chron within each, 2026→2003 | ~35+ journal papers, 4 chapters, 20+ conference items |

**Verdict for this project:** year sections beneath a theme-chip row. Satish has ~39 journal items — too few to need heavy machinery, enough to need a map. Keep Book Chapters as its own small section; move Conference Presentations and Invited Seminars to a **Talks** page; move "Products" to a **Tools** page; drop or fold "Scientific activities" into Service.

### 1.2 Own-name emphasis

Universal pattern: **own name bold, venue italic, title either plain or the link**. Barron bolds "Jon Barron"; Maxwell bolds "**Maxwell, R.M.**"; Sinclair bolds the PI; al-folio *italicises* the owner (configured via `scholar:last_name` / `scholar:first_name` in `_config.yml`, auto-underlined/emphasised) and auto-links co-authors from `_data/coauthors.yml`.

Do it with a slightly heavier weight and full-opacity colour while the rest of the author list sits at ~65% opacity. That reads as emphasis without the crude thickness of `<b>`.

### 1.3 Student co-author marking — the standout detail

Verified legend from https://maxwell.princeton.edu/ :

> `(# indicates postdoc author, * indicates student author, ** indicates undergraduate student author, R.M.Maxwell in bold)`

Real entries:

> `Fleury*, M.P., Ma, Y., and **Maxwell, R.M.** High resolution estimates of water table depth across Brazil: insights into model behavior and data challenges, Environmental Research Letters`
>
> `Abbaszadeh#, P., Zaouna Maina, F., Yang#, C., ... and **Maxwell, R.M.** Coupling the ParFlow Integrated Hydrology Model within the NASA Land Information System`

Note that Sinclair Lab uses `*` for **equal contribution**, not for students — so if we use `*` for students we must say so explicitly in the legend, and if any of Satish's papers use `*` for co-first authorship we need a second symbol. Recommend:

- `*` PhD student
- `†` M.Tech student
- `‡` B.Tech / intern
- `#` postdoc / project staff
- `§` co-first author (only if needed)

Render as a superscript immediately after the surname, in the accent colour at ~0.7em. Legend printed once, small caps, above the first year header, and repeated in a `<details>` at the foot.

**Data model:** don't ask the professor to type symbols. Give the sheet an `author_marks` column, e.g. `1:phd,3:mtech`, meaning author index 1 is a PhD student. Build script inserts symbols. Or simpler: a `students` column listing names, matched against the author string.

### 1.4 Links per paper — styling

Three observed idioms, in descending order of elegance:

1. **Slash-joined lowercase words** (Barron): `project page / arXiv / video / code / bibtex`
2. **Middot-prefixed** (Healy): `· abstract  · pdf`
3. **Arrow-suffixed sentence links** (Heiss): `Full details »`, `Preprint`, `Final version`, `Code`, `Analysis notebook`, `Data`, `Replication Docker container`, `Add to Zotero`

vs. **small buttons** (al-folio: `Abs` `Bib` `DOI` `HTML` `PDF` `Video`) — legible but noisy, and Nicole Paul deliberately renders the same seven link types as flat text with no fill.

**Recommended set for a hydrology site**, in this order, omitting any that don't apply: `doi · pdf · data · code · slides · press · bib`. Note that `data` and `code` are *unusually* valuable here — they signal an open-science practice that most Indian hydrology pages lack, and Satish already produces tools.

### 1.5 Volume, filtering, search

- Client-side text filter over title+authors+journal+year. MIT DLC template labels: `Search publications:`, `Filter by publication type — Select type —`, `Filter by year — Select a year —`, `Reset filters`. Keep the search box, drop the dropdowns (the chips do that job).
- Stanford `~ahmedah/publication-filter-suggestions` recommends starting with a simple two-state **Selected / All** toggle before adding topic tabs, using CSS classes (`selected-paper`, `safety-paper`) toggled by JS. That's the minimum viable version if the theme chips are deferred.
- ★ or a hairline accent rule on the ~6 "selected" papers; the homepage renders only those.

### 1.6 Abstracts, BibTeX, metrics

- **Abstracts:** Barron shows none. Naik's contest-winning site shows none despite being praised for having them. Heiss replaces them with a **haiku**. Mayank Mittal writes a 2–4 sentence plain description. → Write a one-line takeaway for the 6 selected papers only.
- **BibTeX:** al-folio's `Bib` opens an expandable block inline; Mark Dean does the same. jekyll-scholar has an *open feature request* (issue #223) for copy-to-clipboard BibTeX — i.e. it is still not standard, so a small custom `copy` affordance is a genuine differentiator. Generate `.bib` at build time from sheet columns.
- **Metrics:** arXiv:1702.07960 — 129 of 870 physicists (14.8%) at 11 well-known universities displayed citations on personal websites; professors displayed most; h-index display showed no significant institutional/national/rank differences. Satish's Scholar profile (`cTXdUlUAAAAJ`) reports ~1,784 citations. → link, don't print.

---

## 2. PEOPLE

### 2.1 Current group

Satish's existing categories (from his Students page): Current PhD students (with topics), Current M.Tech students (with joining year), Graduated PhD students (thesis title + viva date), M.Tech graduates (thesis title + year), Undergraduate mini-projects (title + year). Co-supervision is already noted inline ("co-supervision", "co-supervisor"). **No photos, no alumni positions.**

Metadata worth carrying per current member, drawn from Cardenas + MSU + Pokhrel:
name · programme (PhD / M.Tech / B.Tech / Project staff / Intern) · cohort/joining year · one-line topic · co-advisor (if any) · optional email / Scholar / personal site · photo.

Cardenas keeps **empty categories visible** — "MS Students (currently none)" — which is honest and keeps the page's shape stable as a group grows and shrinks. Pokhrel's MSU lab adds a **"Visiting Researchers/Interns"** category, directly relevant to an IIT group.

### 2.2 Alumni — three formats observed

**(a) One-line text, parenthetical placement** — Cardenas, https://www.jsg.utexas.edu/cardenas/people/ :
```
Kevin Befus, PhD Geological Sciences, 2015 (Assistant Professor, University of Arkansas)
```
Section headings verbatim: "Former PhD Students, Post-doctoral Fellows, and Visiting Fellows" / "Former MS/MA Students" / "Former Undergraduate Students and REU/RET Fellows".

**(b) Table with sector coding** — UIC Hu Lab, https://hu.lab.uic.edu/alumni/ . Four tables. PhD table columns: `Current position: Academia (A), Industry (I), Government (G)` | `Training period` | `Thesis`. No photos.

**(c) "First placement" only** — BU Material Robotics Lab, https://sites.bu.edu/mrl/alumni . PhDs and postdocs get "first placement: Research and Design Engineer at the Wellman Center for Photomedicine, Massachusetts General Hospital"; most alumni get name + LinkedIn only. Never goes stale.

**(d) Bolded label inline** — MSU FEW Lab, https://water.egr.msu.edu/members/ : `**Current Position**: Postdoctoral scholar at KAUST, Saudi Arabia.` / `**Currently at**: Jacobs Solutions Inc.`

**Recommendation:** (a) as the visual form, with (c)'s data honesty and (b)'s sector coding as an optional column. Concretely:

```
Rahul Sharma*  ·  PhD, Civil Engineering, 2023
Multi-model streamflow forecasting for the Godavari basin
→ Scientist-SD, National Remote Sensing Centre, Hyderabad   [Govt]
```

Above the list, one summary sentence: *"Twelve PhD and M.Tech theses completed since 2017; alumni are at NRSC, CWC, state irrigation departments, IITs, and in industry."*

### 2.3 Photos and fallbacks

Asymmetry across all exemplars: **current members photographed, alumni not**. Adopt it. For missing current-member photos, use a deterministic two-letter initials monogram on a tinted square derived from a hash of the name (DiceBear "initials" style is the reference; setproduct.com/blog/avatar-ui-design: *"Never leave the avatar blank—fallbacks like initials or generic silhouettes preserve the structure of the interface"*). Alt text always present. Photos square with a small radius, greyscale-to-colour on hover is a cliché — skip it.

### 2.4 Ordering

Current: by programme, then by cohort year ascending (senior students first — signals depth). Alumni: reverse-chron by graduation year within programme. Give the sheet an explicit `order` column so the professor can override without touching code.

---

## 3. TEACHING

### 3.1 What Satish has now

A flat bulleted list of ten course names, no codes, no semesters, no levels, no links:
Engineering Hydrology · Open Channel Hydraulics · Fundamentals of RS & GIS · RS & GIS Lab · Fluid Mechanics Lab · Engineering Hydrology and Hydrologic Systems · Applied Computational Laboratory · Hydraulic and Hydrologic Simulation Lab · Climate Monitoring and Variability · RS, GIS and Climate Change.

That is unusable to the person it exists for (a student choosing electives, or a hiring/awards committee).

### 3.2 The best structure found

Heiss, https://www.andrewheiss.com/teaching/ — academic-year sections, one row per course:

```
PMAP 8551/4551 · Data Visualization with R · Georgia State University
Use R, ggplot2, and the principles of graphic design to create beautiful
and truthful visualizations of data.
Fall 2025 · Spring 2026
```
(each semester a link to that semester's course site)

Healy, https://kieranhealy.org/teaching/ — single scroll, explicitly: *"the further you scroll down the page the further into the past you will travel."* Current courses get a paragraph + live site; past courses collapse to title + syllabus PDF. **Progressive decay of detail.**

Najam, https://fawadnajam.com/ — courses archived per offering with the term in the title: `"NUST – CE 809: Structural Dynamics (Fall 2021)"`, `"NUST – CE 809: Structural Dynamics (Fall 2020)"`, plus handwritten notes and video lecture series per course. Good for a teacher who genuinely maintains materials; heavy otherwise.

### 3.3 Teaching philosophy

https://www.colorado.edu/lab/krg/teaching/teaching-philosophy — the working example in exactly Satish's discipline:
- CVEN 4333 Engineering Hydrology, ~100 students, juniors/seniors
- CVEN 5393 Water Resource Systems and Management, ~15–20 graduate students
- CVEN 5423 Water Resources Engineering, mixed UG/grad
- Named tools: RiverWare, Python. Named case study: Colorado River negotiations.
- Mentoring block separate: feedback on communication and public speaking, conference travel, weekly interdisciplinary workshops, a research blog with 100,000+ views.

**Do not link the LMS.** Link a static per-course page here instead: syllabus PDF, topic outline, reading list, public notebooks/datasets. Only build these for 2–3 courses.

### 3.4 Student feedback

None of the strong academic exemplars quoted student evaluations on the public site — Heiss's page has no evaluations section, Healy's has none. Testimonials appeared only on the marketing-listicle sites (themathguru.ca in the founderjar roundup), which is the register to avoid. **Skip student quotes.** If teaching recognition exists (an institute teaching award), put it in Awards.

### 3.5 Outreach, mentoring, service

Maxwell gives "education and outreach" a top-level nav slot naming STEM fairs, teaching at local schools, and the Digital Sandtank tool. Hahm turns outreach into a **press-mentions list** (Scientific American, Nature Geoscience, NYT, 2014–2026). Satish has directly analogous material: water awareness work, "Guidelines for Sixer Twitter", the Rural Development Center chairpersonship (per his LinkedIn — UNVERIFIED from a first-party page), and India-specific flood communication. Give it a short section, not a page, unless the material is substantial.

---

## 4. CV: page vs PDF

Consensus from the search: **one source of record, many renderings.** "Having the CV pull from the same Markdown files as the website eliminates drift between the two." "Keep your full academic CV as the source of record and generate each structured submission from it, never the other way round."

For this project the source of record is the Google Sheets. Build step:
1. Sheets → JSON at build time.
2. JSON → site pages.
3. JSON + a template → CV PDF (Typst, LaTeX, or headless-Chrome print CSS).
4. Stamp both with the build date.

Page copy: `Curriculum Vitae — PDF, updated 4 September 2026`. Healy puts "Full Curriculum Vitae in pdf format" at the top of his publications page, which is the right place for it. Also render a lightweight HTML CV for mobile and SEO — but generated, never hand-typed.

Scilio flags Mark Dean's site as having "No CV or teaching page" as a weakness — so a CV is expected even on a strong group-style site.

---

## 5. NEWS / UPDATES

Format that works (Mark Dean, https://markdean.info/):
```
Aug 23, 2026 — Mark is attending the MAIQmag All Hands Meeting at
Oak Ridge National Laboratory on August 24–25.
Jul 20, 2026 — Our paper introducing simulation-based inference to extract
Hamiltonian parameters ... has been posted to the arXiv.
```
4 items on the homepage, reverse-chron, each 1–2 sentences with a link. al-folio ships the same as a `news` collection; it has a known scrollable-container bug (issue #2658) — avoid an inner scroll region, just cap the count.

Mayank Mittal uses `MMM DD, YYYY` headers; typical items are paper acceptances, awards, talks.

Failure mode (Scilio, on martinbulla.github.io): the "last updated" line itself went stale. Mitigation: generate the footer date at build time, and if updates land less than monthly, replace the feed with a short honest paragraph ("an honest paragraph beats an outdated news feed").

Sheet columns: `date | text | link_url | link_label | pinned`.

---

## 6. AWARDS / HONOURS

None of the exemplars gives awards a top-level page; they appear (a) inline in the bio narrative — Satyanarayan mentions an NSF CAREER award and a Kavli Fellowship in running prose; (b) as an "EDUCATION / EXPERIENCE / RESEARCH INTERESTS"-style block on an About page — Balaji Rajagopalan's structure; (c) attached to individual publications as a ★ badge — vis.mit.edu; or (d) in the CV.

**Recommendation:** a compact `Year — Award — Awarding body` list at the foot of the About page, plus ★ on award-winning papers. No separate nav item unless there are 8+ entries.

---

## 7. TALKS

Nuria Oliver's page (https://nuriaoliver.com/invitedtalks.htm) is instructive mostly as a warning: 300+ talks split into three thematic buckets ("Scientific Conferences and Technical Talks" / "Government, courses, universities and technology conferences" / "General Public Events (TEDx…)"), which destroys chronology and makes recency invisible. Slides and video are rarely linked.

Karpathy (https://karpathy.ai/) does the opposite — "Featured talks" as a **thumbnail gallery** with video links, chronological, small in number.

**Recommendation:** year-grouped rows: `Title (or "Invited seminar") — Host / Conference, City — Month Year` with optional `slides` / `video` links, and a small inline label for `Keynote` / `Plenary`. Source data already exists in his sections D (Presentations at Conferences) and E (Invited Seminars). Consider a "Selected talks" cap of ~15 on the page with the full list in the CV.

---

## 8. DATA / CODE / TOOLS

Reed Maxwell gives `codes` a top-level nav slot for **ParFlow** (integrated watershed flow model) and **EcoSLIM** (Lagrangian particle tracking), each with a description and GitHub link. Heiss offers per-paper `Code`, `Data`, `Analysis notebook`, and `Replication Docker container`. Nicole Paul links `Dataset` to Zenodo/GitHub/institutional handles per paper.

Satish already has (currently buried as "Section A: Products" atop the publications page):
- a climate analysis web tool
- **Hydro-EMOS** — streamflow forecasting diagnostic tool
- a poverty visualization application
- **SnapFlood** (has its own Research subpage)

**Recommendation:** top-level `Tools` section. Per tool: screenshot or a single hero frame, name, one line on *who it is for* (researcher / agency engineer / public), status (live / archived / on request), live link, code link, and the paper it belongs to. This is the site's strongest differentiator against every other Indian hydrology faculty page, and it directly supports his stated goal of "translating research into information and decision-support tools for scientists, engineers, operational agencies, and policymakers."

Ecosystem links worth adding on that page: HydroShare (CUAHSI), and his GitHub if public.

---

## 9. CONTACT + PROSPECTIVE STUDENTS

### 9.1 Contact data must be reconciled first

| Field | Google Site | IITH profile (https://iith.ac.in/ce/satishr/) |
|---|---|---|
| Phone | `+91-40-2301 6315` | `(040) 2359 - 6315` |
| Address | `IIT Hyderabad, Kandi - 502285, India` | `Kandi-502284, Sangareddy, Telangana, India` |
| Office | — | `Room: B-212, Department of Civil Engineering` |
| Email | `satishr.at.iith.ac.in` (obfuscated) | `satishr@ce.iith.ac.in` |

The departmental faculty listing (https://civil.iith.ac.in/people/faculty) gives `satishr@ce.iith.ac.in` and `+91 40 2301-6315`. So the phone is contested even within IITH's own pages. **Ask the professor to confirm; publish one set.** Include Room B-212 — offices are almost never listed and are genuinely useful.

Note also that his site obfuscates the email as `satishr.at.iith.ac.in` while his Opportunities page uses `satishr.at.ce.iith.ac.in` — two different domains. Modern practice: render the real `mailto:` (spam filtering has long since made obfuscation pointless) and be consistent.

### 9.2 Prospective students — the single most-emailed topic

His current Opportunities page already does several things right: it names the areas ("hydroclimatology, rainfall and flood forecasting and modelling, data science, AI/ML, scientific computing"), names the roles (interns, prospective PhD students, postdocs), asks for a specific subject line ("Looking for an Opportunity"), and asks for research interests, background/skills, motivation, and what they hope to learn and contribute.

What the best examples add:

1. **Funding reality, dated and first.** Remote Sensing Hydrology: *"I do not currently have funding for a graduate student"* — only fellowship-funded applicants should apply, with limited advice offered on fellowship applications. Mark Dean: *"We do not currently have open postdoc positions, but interested candidates are welcome to email Mark. We especially welcome postdocs with fellowships, and would be happy to support you in applying both before and after joining our group."*
2. **Named fellowship routes.** Dean lists SNSF (Switzerland), Fulbright (Korea), Goldhaber (BNL). Indian equivalents to name: PMRF, CSIR-JRF / UGC-NET JRF, DST INSPIRE, SERB N-PDF, Fulbright-Nehru, Newton-Bhabha, institute TA-ships and project positions.
3. **A cheap engagement filter.** Remote Sensing Hydrology routes everyone through a Google Form with an optional question: pick one of my papers, read it carefully, answer some questions about it — *"I would encourage you to do that, read it carefully and provide a thoughtful response."* A Google Form is also perfectly aligned with this project's Google-Workspace-centred editing model.
4. **Explicit don'ts.** UVA SRG (https://uvasrg.github.io/prospective/): sections "Who To Contact / Do Your Homework / First Email / What Not To Do / Follow Up". Rules: read the home page and at least one recent paper; keep it to about one screenful; name the paper and where you found it; state one concrete research question; do NOT send GPA/GRE scores, excessive self-promotion, generic flattery, unrelated attachments, or fancy formatting.
5. **Demystify the process.** Yonatan Bisk (https://talkingtorobots.com/FAQ.html) publishes the admissions funnel: rounds 1–2 filter ~50% each, faculty see the remaining ~25%, then shortlist/interview/vote. He also states when to email (*after* applying) and what makes a good recommendation letter ("your ability to work independently, ability to come up with interesting research questions/next steps"). He describes generic mass emails as "DOS attacks."

**Recommended page shape:**
```
Prospective students & postdocs
[dated status line]  As of September 2026 I am / am not recruiting …
Who fits            backgrounds, quantitative expectations
How to apply        IITH admissions link + this form / this email
Your email          subject line (copy button) + 4 bullets of what to include
Before you write    read one paper; name it and one question it raised
What I can't do     review CVs for unrelated programmes; letters for people I haven't taught
Funding routes      PMRF, CSIR/UGC-JRF, INSPIRE, N-PDF, institute TA-ships …
```

## 10. SITE ARCHITECTURE + THE RAFT PROBLEM

Two proven shapes:

- **Thin personal + deep group** — Satyanarayan: three paragraphs and *"Please consult my research group's website for our latest publications and active projects."*
- **Personal that scales into group** — Mark Dean: `About / People / Group notes / Research / Openings / Publications / Preprints` + ctrl-K search, one site doing both jobs.

Since `raftwaters.in` does not currently resolve and will be hosted separately, **satishregonda.in must be the Dean model, not the Satyanarayan model**. It must own the publications, the people, the teaching and the tools. RAFT becomes a rich single page here: what the group is, its mission, a group photo, current members, flagship projects, 3–4 highlight outputs, and a prominent outbound link. If raftwaters.in is ever down, this site still tells the whole story.

Proposed nav (7 items max, which every good exemplar respects):
`Research · Publications · Group · Teaching · Tools · Writing · About` — with Contact folded into About or pinned in the footer, News on the homepage, Talks/Awards/CV under About. His existing IA (Home / Education & Employment / Products & Publications / Research▾ / Teaching / Students / RAFT / Opportunities) has three items that are really CV content and one ("Education & Employment") that should never be a top-level page.

## 11. GOOGLE SHEETS SCHEMA (drives all of the above)

**`publications`** — `id | year | type(journal|chapter|conference|preprint|report) | title | authors | students | journal | volume | pages | doi | pdf_url | code_url | data_url | slides_url | press_url | theme | selected | takeaway | note`

**`people`** — `name | role(phd|mtech|btech|postdoc|staff|intern|visitor) | cohort_year | end_year | status(current|alumni) | topic | thesis_title | co_advisor | photo_file | email | scholar_url | website_url | first_position | current_position | sector(academia|government|industry|other) | order`

**`teaching`** — `code | title | level(btech|mtech|phd) | semesters | description | syllabus_url | site_url | status(current|past) | enrolment`

**`news`** — `date | text | link_url | link_label | pinned`

**`talks`** — `date | title | kind(invited|keynote|plenary|conference) | host | city | slides_url | video_url`

**`tools`** — `name | tagline | audience | status | image | live_url | code_url | paper_id`

Build-time validation should fail loudly on: a `doi` that isn't a DOI, a `photo_file` that doesn't exist, a `students` name not present in `authors`, a `selected` count above ~8. That is what makes a non-technical editor safe.

## 12. Low-signal source, flagged

https://www.founderjar.com/inspiration/academic-website-examples/ lists 26 "academic website examples" but is a marketing listicle: its praise is for parallax scrolling, hero animations, image sliders, hamburger-only navigation and testimonial sections. I did not fetch any of the 26 individually and none is cited as an exemplar. Its recommendations are actively wrong for a research site. Treat https://www.scilio.app/examples and https://theacademicdesigner.com/2025/winners-of-the-best-personal-academic-websites-contest-2025/ as the higher-signal roundups — both name real URLs with specific, checkable critique.
